title: Test an unknown-column Polygraphia III recovery search against the known-column baseline
statement: A simple blinded frequency-ranking search, given the true column of every ciphertext token but no plaintext or letter assignment, only partially recovers held-out Latin plaintext. Across four overlapping plaintext windows, mean character accuracy is 0.457/0.474 for 10 columns, 0.345/0.335 for 24, and 0.169/0.167 for 131, for random/sequential columns respectively. This is a weak-search optimistic baseline, not a security bound. Empirical comparison with within-column shuffled held-out ciphertext detects bigram structure in most of these examples; independent iid controls illustrate false positives but are too few to estimate a general rate.
check: Implement an attack without oracle column identifiers and evaluate learned replacement tables and held-out plaintext over many independent plaintext sources, keys and column-selection strategies. Benchmark the frequency search against a contextual optimization, use independent simulation seeds and fully separated texts, and calibrate held-out detection against structured non-language decoys as well as iid text. State search budget, oracle information and treatment of same-spelling table collisions; do not claim a cipher cell is ruled out until the blinded search cracks its calibrated controls.
method: Use Hermes repository P.III table at commit 0ef1439fa9d90aeab42951a51d0d5a0e27db1f8f, SHA-256 fe3f24a46dbc6b655eab8dbbd75addf84ee4a7dbd387ad802af75d02edfe5b4d, first 10, 24, or all 131 rows. Assign permuted hidden row IDs, then choose a row uniformly at random or cycle sequentially, independently of plaintext. Latin reference frequencies and add-one bigram model use refcorpus.train_text; planted plaintext uses refcorpus.control_text, with spaces dropped and v/j normalized by the project. 12,000 training ciphertext tokens and 4,000 following held-out tokens. Decoder sees only ciphertext strings and oracle column IDs in train; per column it ranks ciphertext types by frequency and pairs them with the external Latin letter-frequency ranking. It never sees the true table, training plaintext, or held-out plaintext. Search budget: one ranking per column, no restarts. Score per-character held-out accuracy against truth, compatible mappings for observed train types, and bigram log loss. For a toy false-positive check, generate iid letters from the reference unigram distribution, fit and score the same way. Compare held-out decoded bigram loss with 19 shuffles of test ciphertext within true columns, add-one lower-tail p; cutoff .05. The decision rule and 12 additional iid seeds were chosen after the initial pilot, so not preregistered.
source: Jürgen Hermes, Polygraphia III: The cipher that pretends to be an artificial language, https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3313/paper7.pdf; table https://github.com/hermesj/R_Voynich_Stats/blob/0ef1439fa9d90aeab42951a51d0d5a0e27db1f8f/R%20code/Historical_ciphers/keys/ciphers_poly_III_in_order.csv

reproduce.instructions: Save the script as /tmp/voy_piii_recovery.py and the exact table as /tmp/voy-piii.csv; verify the table SHA-256 above. Run PYTHONPATH=. python3 /tmp/voy_piii_recovery.py. To reproduce additional iid tests import the script and run experiment(n, mode, seed, True) for n in (10,24,131), mode in (random,sequential), seed in range(101,113).
reproduce.script:
import csv, json, random, hashlib, math
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from vs import refcorpus

SEEDS=(13,29,47,71)
TRAIN_N=12000
TEST_N=4000
PATH='/tmp/voy-piii.csv'
raw=open(PATH,'rb').read()
table=list(csv.DictReader(raw.decode('utf-8-sig').splitlines()))
letters=list(table[0]); allowed=set(letters)
for row in table:
    for k in row: row[k]=row[k].strip()
reference=''.join(c for b in refcorpus.train_text('latin') for c in b if c in allowed)
plaintext=''.join(c for b in refcorpus.control_text('latin') for c in b if c in allowed)
prior=Counter(reference); ranking=sorted(letters,key=lambda c:(-prior[c],c))
big=Counter(zip(reference,reference[1:])); prev=Counter(reference[:-1]); m=len(letters)
def nll(s):
    return -sum(math.log2((big[a,b]+1)/(prev[a]+m)) for a,b in zip(s,s[1:]))/max(len(s)-1,1)

def experiment(ncol,mode,seed,iid=False):
    rnd=random.Random(seed); text=plaintext[(seed-13)*180:(seed-13)*180+TRAIN_N+TEST_N]
    if iid: text=''.join(rnd.choices(letters,weights=[prior[c] for c in letters],k=TRAIN_N+TEST_N))
    assert len(text)==TRAIN_N+TEST_N
    # Independent randomized column IDs are supplied to the search as an oracle.
    cols=list(range(ncol)); rnd.shuffle(cols)
    ci=[rnd.randrange(ncol) if mode=='random' else i%ncol for i in range(len(text))]
    observations=[(cols[c],table[cols[c]][p]) for c,p in zip(ci,text)]
    counts=defaultdict(Counter)
    for col,token in observations[:TRAIN_N]: counts[col][token]+=1
    # Search budget is one frequency ranking per known column; no plaintext is provided.
    key={}
    for col,c in counts.items():
        for token,guess in zip(sorted(c,key=lambda t:(-c[t],t)),ranking): key[col,token]=guess
    fallback=ranking[0]
    held=observations[TRAIN_N:]; truth=text[TRAIN_N:]
    guesses=''.join(key.get(x,fallback) for x in held)
    pairs=set(held); known=sum(x in key for x in held)
    correct=sum(a==b for a,b in zip(guesses,truth))
    table_agree=sum(all(table[c][p]==tok for p in [pred]) for (c,tok),pred in key.items())
    # Shuffle ciphertext tokens *within oracle columns* in the test section. Preserve symbol and column marginals.
    shuffled=list(held); groups=defaultdict(list)
    for i,(c,t) in enumerate(held): groups[c].append(i)
    for ids in groups.values():
        vals=[held[i][1] for i in ids]; rnd.shuffle(vals)
        for i,tok in zip(ids,vals): shuffled[i]=(held[i][0],tok)
    decoy=''.join(key.get(x,fallback) for x in shuffled)
    null_nll=[nll(decoy)]
    for _ in range(18):
        shuffled=list(held)
        for ids in groups.values():
            vals=[held[i][1] for i in ids]; rnd.shuffle(vals)
            for i,tok in zip(ids,vals): shuffled[i]=(held[i][0],tok)
        null_nll.append(nll(''.join(key.get(x,fallback) for x in shuffled)))
    p=(1+sum(x<=nll(guesses) for x in null_nll))/20
    return {'ncol':ncol,'strategy':mode,'seed':seed,'iid_plaintext':iid,'empirical_tail_p':p,'train_tokens':TRAIN_N,'test_tokens':TEST_N,
      'types_learned':len(key),'learned_table_cells_compatible':table_agree,'test_types':len(pairs),
      'test_seen_fraction':round(known/len(held),4),'test_accuracy':round(correct/len(held),4),
      'null_accuracy_against_original_plaintext':round(sum(a==b for a,b in zip(decoy,truth))/len(truth),4),
      'test_bigram_nll':round(nll(guesses),4),'decoy_bigram_nll':round(nll(decoy),4),'true_bigram_nll':round(nll(truth),4)}

if __name__ == '__main__':
    result={'table_sha256':hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest(),'total_columns':len(table),'alphabet':letters,
            'reference_chars':len(reference),'control_chars':len(plaintext),'prior_rank':ranking,
            'rows':[experiment(n,mode,s,iid) for n in (10,24,131) for mode in ('random','sequential') for s in SEEDS for iid in (False,True)]}
    print(json.dumps(result,indent=2))

limitations: The plaintext windows overlap substantially and are from one corpus, so the four trials are not independent generalization evidence. Column identity is an oracle, and each column supplies at most one codeword per plaintext letter; neither assumption necessarily holds in a target manuscript. The published table contains cross-column collisions and at least one within-column collision; a mapping is called compatible when its assigned letter produces that spelling, and character accuracy is checked against the actual plaintext. The iid null and 19-permutation test are small pilot controls, not a robust false-positive calibration; the detection rule was selected after seeing exploratory data. The known published table is used only by the generator and evaluator. The task’s unknown-column recovery and strong false-positive evaluation remain open.
